newsitem.title: USA: Dlr ends strong in US but off multi-year highs.
newsitem.headline: Dlr ends strong in US but off multi-year highs.

text.p: The dollar closed higher on Monday, continuing to benefit from the contrast of sturdy U.S. economic growth against languishing overseas economies.

The dollar set a series of fresh multi-year highs early Monday, after another dramatic drop in Japan's stock market further eroded confidence in yen investments, while remarks from two Bundesbank members highlighted German economic woes.

But, after reaching 118.29 yen and 1.6315 marks in European trade, the dollar's best levels since March 1993 and June 1994 respectively, the rally fizzled in the U.S. where staffing was light for the Martin Luther King Jr holiday.
"There was a little bit of action, mostly centered in Europe," said Stephen Jury, chief dealer at Union Bank of Switzerland. "The New York end of things is very quiet."

Trade activity in New York nearly evaporated shortly after noontime. At 1400 EST/1900 GMT the dollar was quoted at 118.08/18 yen, up from 117.82/87 at the open and at 1.6280/90 marks, up from 1.6255/65 marks.
The dollar also scored a 31-month high at 1.4205 swiss francs on Monday, before settling at 1.4175/85 Swiss, up from 1.4140/50.
Traders are increasingly viewing dollar investments as a can't-lose bet, while evidence that the U.S. economy entered 1997 in excellent fitness continues to mount.
"They do have an appetite to buy dollars on dips," said Susan Stearns, a director of foreign exchange at Bank of Montreal in New York.
"It appears that those who are buying dollars are also wearing diamonds," she added jokingly.

The latest bits of good news for the U.S. came on Friday when government data on December industrial activity and the November international trade deficit prompted many Wall Street economists to revise their fourth-quarter economic growth forecasts upwards.

At the same time, the ferocious decline in Japan's Nikkei 225 stock average, which dropped another 609.70 points on Monday, has prompted selling of Japanese shares by foreign investors, who continue to convert the yen proceeds into other units like the dollar.

Meanwhile, in an article in the International Herald Tribune on Monday, Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer drew attention to Germany's economic troubles by warning that Germany's faltering economic recovery was not yet self-sustaining.
In a speech on Monday, another Bundesbank policy-maker, Hans-Juergen Krupp, also chimed in, saying German financial policy is "hindering still continuing economic recovery."
"Some more weak economic data is expected from Germany, which will support potentially another repo cut -- I think that is the idea," said David Gilmore, partner at Foreign Exchange Analytics.
Elsewhere, the dollar fell to Canadian $1.3367/72 from C$1.3385/90 at the open, and the pound closed at $1.6620/30 little changed from $1.6618/28.
The Australian dollar was at $0.7765/70 in late trade, compared to $0.7770/75 at the open.
